owner.occupation: PhD candidate in Chinese literature at a Paris university

world.bio: I am a PhD candidate in Chinese literature at a Paris university. My thesis is on late-Qing popular narratives, and I am translating an obscure novella whose only surviving printed edition breaks off before the ending. I live with three flatmates in a tiny apartment and play bass in a jazz trio on Thursdays.
skills_assets: Reading fluency in classical and modern Chinese; translation experience into French
Access to the university library, BnF, and Inalco collections
A trio bass, a decent amp, and weekly gigs in a small bar
A digital archive of scans and notes on late-Qing fiction
Co-author of one published article on serialised novels

projects.name: Translation of 'The Plum Blossom Pawnshop' (梅花当)
projects.text: A late-Qing novella from the 1890s. My translation stops at chapter 18 because the only surviving 1890s edition is missing its last pages. I have the text up to a mid-sentence in chapter 18 and nothing after. I do not know whether later editions exist, or whether another library holds a complete copy.

projects.name: Thesis chapter on popular narrative
projects.text: Chapter three is about pawnshop motifs in Qing fiction. The chapter works without the ending but my supervisor wants the translation as an appendix.

notes.text: Library day. Spent four hours with the scans of 梅花当. The last printed page ends mid-sentence: '當鋪的掌櫃嘆了口氣道，這件事……' and that is it. Eighteen chapters and no ending. I keep reading that sentence like it is a joke.
Flatmate Louise burned the soup. We opened every window. Rehearsal tonight, the drummer was late, as always.
Emailed a librarian in Shanghai about 梅花当. No answer yet. Emailed one in Taipei too. Silence. Maybe they are on holiday.

Supervisor asked how the translation was going. I said eighteen chapters done. He asked how many chapters in total. I said I don't know, the preface says twenty-four. He said you have to find the ending. I said I am trying.
Funding ends next summer. I need to finish by then or find a teaching job. Both feel impossible tonight.
Gig at Le Petit Duc: forty people, one good solo. Walked home along the Seine in the rain. Felt briefly like a person.
Flatmates want to move out in January. I will have to find another place. Paris is brutal.
Read a chapter of the novella again for the tenth time, trying to infer how it ends. The pawnshop owner, the stolen jade, the daughter. Something must happen. I just don't know what.

messages.text: Supervisor: Any progress on the ending? Me: I've asked librarians in Shanghai and Taipei. Supervisor: Try Beijing too. Me: I will.
Tom: Rehearsal Thursday? Me: Yes. Tom: Bring the new tune. Me: I'm still learning it.
Louise: Rent is due. Me: I know. Louise: Also the soup. Me: I'm sorry.
Mum: Are you eating? Me: Yes. Mum: When are you home? Me: Christmas. Mum: Good.
Jin: Did you hear back from Shanghai? Me: No. Jin: Maybe they don't have it. Me: Maybe nobody does.

relations.about: Senior professor of Chinese literature, kind but vague.
Chinese student at the same lab, helps with tricky passages.
Lives in Lyon, worried about money.

constraints: Cannot travel to China without grants
Does not read the traditional-character cursive hand easily
